parts.text: I want Skyrim RP. I was a regular teenager, 16, really liked to play this game after school, went through several times, collecting all unique things, collected and read all books (with mod that added books even from all other parts of series). And now I open my eyes. Body is mine and not mine at the same time - my all-time character that was my avatar in every playthrough (game created model, so obviously no wounds or imperfections, no relatives or any history behind), but with my face, younger (models are represented adult). I have nothing on me, just simple clothes. I wake on the side of road
Before I open your eyes — three things I need to know, because in Skyrim your body decides how the world greets you long before your words do.

questions.question: What race was your all-time character? (The face is yours — the rest isn't.)

options.label: Nord
options.description: You pass as local. Cold doesn't bite. Nobody asks where you're from — which cuts both ways when you have no answers.

options.label: Imperial or Breton
options.description: Human, foreign, unremarkable. Merchants like you. Stormcloaks don't.

options.label: Mer — Altmer, Bosmer, or Dunmer
options.description: Doors close. Guards watch. You'd better be worth the trouble.

options.label: Khajiit or Argonian
options.description: Barred from cities. Sleeping outside walls. The hardest possible start.

questions.question: What did you always play? (Your MIND remembers every perk. This 16-year-old body remembers nothing — but bone, reach and reflex are still shaped by the model you chose.)

options.label: Stealth archer
options.description: Light frame, long fingers, quiet feet. The eternal Skyrim classic.

options.label: Two-hander / sword-and-board
options.description: Broad shoulders on a boy who's never swung anything heavier than a schoolbag.

options.label: Mage
options.description: Nothing physical to fall back on. But you know the words. Do the words know you?

options.label: Spellsword / jack-of-all-trades
options.description: Good at everything, master of nothing — and right now, master of nothing is the operative half.

questions.question: How hard do you want Skyrim to hit?

options.label: Gritty survival
options.description: Hunger, cold, infection, and wolves that actually kill 16-year-olds. Your knowledge is your only edge, and it's a thin one.

options.label: Balanced
options.description: Dangerous but fair. Consequences stick, but the story gives you room to be clever.

options.label: Heroic
options.description: Lean into the power fantasy. You know where every unique item on Tamriel sits. Go get them.

answers.customResponse: I always played Breton (and my real face probably looks like one for locals)

parts.text:
# THE ROAD

Cold, first. Not the cold of a window left open — the cold of *ground*, seeping up through a thin layer of cloth into your shoulder blade and hip.

Then the smell. Pine resin, wet stone, woodsmoke from somewhere far off, and underneath it all a sharp mineral tang like the air before snow. No dust, no laundry detergent, no radiator. Nothing your nose has ever filed away.

You open your eyes.

Grey sky, broken by branches. Not the branches you know — these are the black-green spires of Falkreath pines, tall and close-packed, needles drooping under old snow that hasn't melted since it fell. A single leaf spirals down past your face and lands on your chest, and you watch it settle with the specific slow calm of someone whose brain has not yet caught up to itself.

Then it does. All at once.

---

You sit up too fast and the world tips. You're on the shoulder of a road — real cobblestones, uneven, moss in the seams, worn into two shallow ruts by cartwheels. Grass and stone verge, then trees. The road climbs south behind you into higher ground; north it drops away, and through a gap in the pines you can see, very far off, a pale ribbon of river and beyond it something impossible — a mountain so vast it doesn't read as a mountain, it reads as a *wall the sky is leaning against*. Seven thousand steps of it.

You know that mountain. You have climbed it in a loading screen.

You look down at your hands.

They're wrong. They're wrong in the way a photograph of yourself is wrong — familiar and alien at once. Long-fingered. Pale in the Breton way. And *clean*. Not washed-clean: **unused**. No calluses. No nicks from a kitchen knife. The half-moon scar you got on your left thumb at nine years old, closing a bike lock — gone. The nails are perfect and identical, ten little copies of the same asset.

Your arms are longer than they should be. Your shoulders sit wider. When you touch your face you find your own — your nose, the shape of your jaw, the mole under your left eye, all of it *yours* — set into a stranger's head on a stranger's neck. Sixteen years of your face on a body that was built, not born, and then scaled down to fit you like a coat bought a size too big to grow into.

You're wearing a roughspun tunic, coarse and undyed, and footwraps. That's it. No boots. No pack. No coin purse, no dagger, no ring, no lockpicks, nothing sewn into a hem. You check anyway, twice, because a part of you is still expecting a menu.

There isn't one. There's just the cold, and a pulse hammering in a throat that has never been afraid before, and the very specific, very useless knowledge that you are somewhere in Falkreath Hold in the year 4E 201 — and that the roughspun tunic and footwraps you are wearing are, item for item, what the Empire issues to a man it intends to behead.

---

Your Breton body has a Breton body's inheritance whether you earned it or not: magicka sits in you like a held breath, and there's a thin, cool resistance under your skin, the kind that shrugs off a frost spell at the edges. Whether you can *use* any of it is another question entirely. Your mind knows two hundred hours of muscle memory. Your muscles know nothing. You have never swung anything heavier than a schoolbag.

You're maybe three, four minutes into being alive here when you hear it.

Down the road, from the south — the direction of the high pass — hooves on cobblestone. More than one horse. And under the hooves, the dry rattle of iron-shod wheels. A wagon. Maybe several. Coming up the road toward you at a walking pace, still out of sight around the bend, but not far.

There is a ditch on the far side of the road, deep enough with the grass grown high over it.

You have about twenty seconds to decide.

**What do you do?**
*I stand up and wait on the road*

You stand.

It takes longer than it should. Your legs come up under you like borrowed furniture — the knees lock a half-second late, the balance arrives after the movement, and you sway once on the verge before the road agrees to hold still. *Too tall.* Your eyeline is a full head above where your body files it. The ground looks further away than it has any right to.

Bare soles on wet cobble. It's like standing on ice.

You plant yourself on the shoulder of the road, hands open and out from your sides, and you wait — because running means being chased, and there's nowhere to run *to* when you don't have shoes, a map, or a single coin.

The cart comes round the bend.

Not the Imperial carts. Thank every Divine you can name and several you can't — it's a farm wagon, high-sided, stacked with split birch under a lashed tarp, drawn by a heavy grey horse with feathered hooves and a bored expression. A woman drives it: fifty-something, Nord, sun-cracked at the eyes, a fur cloak pinned at one shoulder and a hand-axe wedged into the bench beside her thigh, not for show.

And riding at the tail of the wagon, on a bay gelding — a **Falkreath guard**. Full kit. The hold's colors under a mail shirt, that flat-topped helm with the nose-guard that makes everyone's face a slit. He sees you first.

The horse stops. The wagon stops. Everything stops.

You watch the guard's eyes track you top to bottom, and you can *read the arithmetic happening behind the nose-guard*, because it's the same arithmetic you'd do:

Roughspun tunic, undyed. Footwraps, no boots. No pack, no belt, no purse, no blade. A young man — tall, whole, well-fed, clean — standing alone on the Falkreath road at first light, dressed exactly the way the Empire dresses a man before it puts him in a cart.

The guard's hand goes to his axe haft. Doesn't draw. Just rests there.

"**Stand where you are.**"

The woman on the bench doesn't reach for her hand-axe, which tells you something. She leans forward instead, squinting, and her mouth does something complicated.

"Divines. He's a *boy*." A pause. "Where are your shoes, lad?"

"He's a *Breton*," the guard says, like that's a separate charge on the same indictment. To you, louder: "Name. Hold. And how you came to be standing on the Falkreath road in a prisoner's rag with no boots on your feet."

He walks the gelding three steps closer. Not enough to be in reach. Enough to be in *reach* if he wants to be.

"There's been Imperials on this road two days running," he says. "Whole column came down out of Darkwater with a catch worth a jarldom, and they took the pass east of here before dawn. Anyone missing off one of their carts is going to be missed *loudly*." The helm tilts. "So. Are you a runaway, a thief, or a liar? Pick early. It goes easier."

---

*Your mind, meanwhile, is screaming.*

*Darkwater. A catch worth a jarldom. Column through the pass before dawn, heading east into Falkreath Hold, toward the one fort-town in these mountains that you know the name of the way you know your own address.*

*It's today. It might be happening this hour. Somewhere behind the treeline to the east there is a stone keep with a headsman's block in the square, and a man in a gag who is going to lose his head, and something with wings coming out of the north to make sure he doesn't.*

*You know exactly how many people die at Helgen. You know what the sky looks like when it happens.*

*You are barefoot, unarmed, sixteen, and standing in front of a man with an axe who wants a name.*

---

The cold is starting to be a real problem. Your feet have gone from painful to numb, which is worse. There's an emptiness under your ribs that you recognize, distantly, as the beginning of being genuinely hungry — not skipped-lunch hungry. The other kind.

The woman is still watching you. The guard is waiting.

**What do you say?**
*I say the thruth. At least part of it* "I don't know. One moment I was sleeping in my bed, the other I wake up somewhere in the wilderness, with nothing on me. And my name is Ray Ebonarm."

You tell them the truth. Or the part of it that fits in a mouth.

"I don't know." Your voice comes out and it's *yours* — that's a small mercy and a strange one, your own voice in this throat. "One moment I was sleeping in my bed. The next I wake up out here. Nothing on me."

The guard says nothing.

"My name is Ray." A beat, and then, because the character sheet answers before you do, because you typed it a hundred times into a box that never once pushed back: "**Ray Ebonarm.**"

---

The effect is not what you expect.

The woman on the bench makes a small sound — *hah* — and claps a hand over her mouth like she's been caught laughing in a temple. The guard's head comes up sharply, and for the first time since he stopped, he takes his hand *off* the axe.

"Ebonarm," he repeats. Flat.

"*Ebonarm,*" the woman says from the bench, delighted, horrified. "Bloody cheek on this one."

You feel the ground shift under a thing you thought was solid. You gave it no thought at all — it was a cool word, it sounded like a warrior, you were twelve when you first typed it and you never changed it because it was *the character's name.*

It is, you now discover, not a name.

"Lad." The guard pushes the helm back off his brow with a thumb, and under it he's younger than the armor suggested, maybe thirty, with a bad shave and tired eyes. "Do you know what you just said to me?"

You don't answer, which is its own answer.

"Ebonarm's a *god*. Black-arm. The Sword-God. They keep his shrines all down the Iliac, your lot do — your grandmother would've cuffed you for it." He looks at you with an entirely new expression, and it is worse than suspicion. It is **pity**. "That's like calling yourself Ray Talos. Ray Akatosh."

"Ray *Stendarr*," the woman offers helpfully.

"Thank you, Hulda."

"Ray Dibella. He's got the face for it."

"*Thank you, Hulda.*"

The guard swings down off the gelding. Boots on cobble. He's shorter than you — your borrowed body has half a head on him — and somehow that makes no difference whatsoever to the balance of power between you.

"Here's what I see," he says, close enough now that you can smell horse and old sweat and oiled steel. "I see a boy in prisoner's cloth with soft hands and no boots, who doesn't know where he is, who's lost his own name and grabbed a god's out of the air to plug the hole." He points, and you follow his finger up the road to the east, where the pines swallow the pass. "Two days ago a Thalmor party came through that gap. Elves in black, and a wagon with the sides shuttered. Nobody's said what was in it and nobody in Falkreath was fool enough to ask."

Cold that has nothing to do with the road goes through you.

"Boys go into those wagons. What comes out doesn't always remember its own bed." He lets that sit. "So. Either you're skooma-addled, or you're mad, or someone's been at your head. And of those three, only one of them's your fault."

He steps back. Looks at your feet — blue-white on the wet stone, no longer feeling anything, which he clearly recognizes as bad.

"Hulda's hauling wood to Falkreath. It's an hour down." He says it to the ground, not to you, the way men say things they'd rather not be quoted on. "You'll ride the tail. I'll not have a frozen corpse on my stretch of road; the Jarl's steward writes *letters*."

Hulda is already unlashing a corner of the tarp. She pulls out a bundle — sacking, tied with cord — and tosses it down at your feet without ceremony.

"Wrap them," she says. "Tight, over the wraps. It's not boots but it's not *nothing*, and you'll lose toes before Falkreath else." She squints down at you. "And when we get there, boy, you keep that name behind your teeth. Falkreath's a hold full of graves and priests of Arkay, and they've no humor at all about the gods."

---

You bend to pick up the sacking and your body does the thing again — the too-long reach, the delay between want and *have*. But your fingers know the knot. Some part of this frame has tied cord before, even if you haven't.

While you wrap, your mind runs the numbers, and they are not good numbers.

*Falkreath. West of Helgen, maybe two hours by cart the other way. An hour south of here on the road means I'm going the WRONG DIRECTION. And the column came through before dawn.*

*It's already happening. Or it's about to. And there is nothing on this Nirn I could do about it — I have no shoes, no weapon, no legs, and even if I ran east right now the only thing waiting for me at Helgen is a burning town and a dragon and the exact death I'd deserve for showing up to it.*

*So let it burn. Let Alduin do his job. Because the second that black shape comes over the mountain, every single thing I know becomes worth something — and until then I'm a barefoot beggar who can't prove a word of it.*

*Falkreath. Fine. Falkreath has an alchemist. Falkreath has a Jarl with a steward who takes letters. Falkreath has —*

Your hands stop on the cord.

*— Falkreath has a shack outside the walls with a boy in it who's about to ask a stranger to kill his mother.*

*And Falkreath has a barrow full of draugr with a unique blade in it that nobody's touched for four thousand years, and I know which room it's in.*

The guard is remounting. Hulda is gathering the reins.

"Well?" she says. "Up, or stay. I'm not paid to wait."

---

The tail-board is down. It's a bare hour to Falkreath, jolting, cold, with a guard riding behind you the whole way who has decided you are either a victim or a lunatic and hasn't fully ruled out *dangerous*.

An hour is a long time. Long enough to be asked more questions. Long enough to ask a few.

**What do you do on the ride — and what, if anything, do you say when they ask you again where you're from?**
